definitions.definition: A Latin phrase meaning 'the end of the self' — the point where a system hits its own limits and cannot save itself.
definitions.example: Like a video game character that can't jump over its own shadow.

definitions.definition: When different ideas or fields lead to the same conclusion without planning it.
definitions.example: Like three friends from different schools all wearing the same shirt on the same day.

definitions.definition: Overwhelmingly powerful or destructive in argument.
definitions.example: Like finding out your favorite superhero's secret weakness.

definitions.definition: A proof that a logical system that works correctly cannot prove its own correctness from inside itself.
definitions.example: Like a scale that can't weigh itself to check if it's accurate.

definitions.definition: Not having any contradictions; everything fits together.
definitions.example: Like a story where the hero doesn't suddenly forget their own name.

definitions.definition: A set of rules and symbols used to do math or logic in a strict way.
definitions.example: Like the rules of chess, but for numbers and statements.

definitions.definition: Basic starting rules that are accepted as true without proof.
definitions.example: Like 'if A equals B and B equals C, then A equals C'.

definitions.definition: A conclusion reached by reasoning from evidence.
definitions.example: Like seeing wet grass and inferring it rained.

definitions.definition: Proving yourself correct using only your own rules.
definitions.example: Like a student grading their own test and giving themselves an A.

definitions.definition: A proof that a language cannot define what 'true' means using only its own words without creating a paradox.
definitions.example: Like trying to define the word 'definition' using only a dictionary that hasn't been written yet.

definitions.definition: A way to say whether a statement is true or false within a system.
definitions.example: Like a computer program that checks if its own output is correct.

definitions.definition: A statement that contradicts itself and can't be true or false.
definitions.example: Like 'This sentence is false' — if it's true, it's false, and if it's false, it's true.

definitions.definition: A classic paradox: 'This statement is false.' It can't be true or false without breaking logic.
definitions.example: Like a sign that says 'Ignore this sign' — you can't follow it.

definitions.definition: Something outside a system used to check or measure it.
definitions.example: Like using a ruler from the store to check if your homemade ruler is accurate.

definitions.definition: A proof that no computer can always predict whether any program will stop or run forever.
definitions.example: Like trying to write a test that can tell if any homework will ever be finished.

definitions.definition: A step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem.
definitions.example: Like a recipe for baking a cake.

definitions.definition: Complex, advanced, or highly developed.
definitions.example: Like a smartphone compared to a flip phone.

definitions.definition: A problem that no computer, no matter how powerful, can solve.
definitions.example: Like trying to write a program that can predict every random coin flip.

definitions.definition: A law of physics saying that in a closed system, disorder (entropy) always increases over time.
definitions.example: Like your room getting messier on its own without you cleaning it.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system.
definitions.example: Like the number of ways a pile of Legos can be scattered vs. built into a castle.

definitions.definition: A system that doesn't exchange energy or matter with anything outside.
definitions.example: Like a sealed thermos with the lid screwed on tight.

definitions.definition: A rule that erasing information always releases a tiny amount of heat, linking computing to physics.
definitions.example: Like how deleting a file on your computer actually warms up the room a tiny bit.

definitions.definition: A minimum amount of energy that must be spent, no matter how efficient the process.
definitions.example: Like the gas you must burn to drive a car, even if it's the most fuel-efficient car ever.

definitions.definition: A unit of energy, like a measure of heat or work.
definitions.example: Like the energy needed to lift a small apple one meter off the ground.

definitions.definition: Related to heat, energy, and work.
definitions.example: Like how a refrigerator uses energy to keep food cold.

definitions.definition: A specific area of knowledge or activity.
definitions.example: Like the 'domain' of biology covers living things.

definitions.definition: A system trying to create a perfect copy of itself inside itself.
definitions.example: Like a computer trying to run a perfect simulation of itself on itself.

definitions.definition: Able to keep itself going without outside help.
definitions.example: Like a plant that gets all its energy from the sun and soil.

definitions.definition: Cannot be undone or reversed.
definitions.example: Like scrambling an egg — you can't unscramble it.

definitions.definition: Continuing to exist or happen over time.
definitions.example: Like the sun rising every morning for billions of years.

definitions.definition: Logical, consistent, and making sense together.
definitions.example: Like a story where all the details fit and don't contradict each other.

definitions.definition: An endless chain where each thing depends on the next, with no starting point.
definitions.example: Like saying 'I need a friend to help me make a friend, but I need a friend to get that friend' — forever.

definitions.definition: The foundation or basis that makes something true or real.
definitions.example: Like the concrete foundation that keeps a house from sinking.

definitions.definition: Something accepted as true with no explanation or reason.
definitions.example: Like saying 'the sky is blue just because it is' and refusing to explain why.

definitions.definition: The idea that everything must have a reason or explanation for why it is the way it is.
definitions.example: Like if your phone is on the table, there's a reason you put it there.

definitions.definition: Cannot be proven wrong, even in principle.
definitions.example: Like saying 'an invisible unicorn lives in my closet' — you can't prove it's not there.

definitions.definition: Something that is its own foundation and doesn't need anything else to exist or be true.
definitions.example: Like a superhero who is their own power source and doesn't need a battery.

definitions.definition: Something that must exist and cannot not exist.
definitions.example: Like the number 2 — it has to exist for math to work.

definitions.definition: Existing by its own nature, not created or dependent on anything else.
definitions.example: Like a computer program that writes itself and runs on its own.

definitions.definition: Having no beginning or end; existing forever.
definitions.example: Like a number line that goes on forever in both directions.

definitions.definition: The quality of being self-existent and not dependent on anything else.
definitions.example: Like a flashlight that powers itself and never needs batteries.

definitions.definition: The idea that God is not made of parts and cannot be divided.
definitions.example: Like a single point of pure light, not a machine with pieces.

definitions.definition: The ultimate foundation that makes everything else exist.
definitions.example: Like the soil that all plants grow from.

definitions.definition: Traditional qualities assigned to God, like being all-powerful, all-knowing, and eternal.
definitions.example: Like saying God is the ultimate source of everything, like the sun is the source of light.
